{{Short description|Theorem in mathematical analysis}}
{{distinguish|Gagliardo–Nirenberg–Sobolev inequality}}
In [[mathematics]], and in particular in [[mathematical analysis]], the '''Gagliardo–Nirenberg interpolation inequality''' is a result in the theory of [[Sobolev space]]s that relates the <math> L^p</math>-norms of different [[weak derivative]]s of a function through an [[interpolation inequality]]. The theorem is of particular importance in the framework of elliptic [[partial differential equation]]s and was originally formulated by [[Emilio Gagliardo]] and [[Louis Nirenberg]] in 1958. The Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality has found numerous applications in the investigation of nonlinear partial differential equations, and has been generalized to fractional Sobolev spaces by [[Haïm Brezis]] and [[Petru Mironescu]] in the late 2010s.

== History ==
The Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality was originally proposed by Emilio Gagliardo and Louis Nirenberg in two independent contributions during the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] held in [[Edinburgh]] from August 14, 1958, through August 21, 1958.<ref name="EG58">{{cite conference |last=Gagliardo |first=Emilio |date=August 14–21, 1958 |title=Propriétés de certaines classes de fonctions de <math> n </math> variables. |url=https://www.mathunion.org/fileadmin/ICM/Proceedings/ICM1958/ICM1958.ocr.pdf |conference=International Congress of Mathematicians |language=fr |location=Edinburgh |page=xxiv}}</ref><ref name="LN58">{{cite conference |last=Nirenberg |first=Louis |date=August 14–21, 1958 |title=Inequalities for derivatives. |url=https://www.mathunion.org/fileadmin/ICM/Proceedings/ICM1958/ICM1958.ocr.pdf |conference=International Congress of Mathematicians |language=en-us |location=Edinburgh |page=xxvii}}</ref> In the following year, both authors improved their results and published them independently.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gagliardo |first=Emilio |date=1958 |title=Proprietà di alcune classi di funzioni in più variabili |journal=Ricerche di Matematica |volume=7 |issue=1 |pages=102–137 |language=it}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gagliardo |first=Emilio |date=1959 |title=Ulteriori proprietà di alcune classi di funzioni di più variabili |journal=Ricerche di Matematica |volume=8 |pages=24–51 |language=it}}</ref><ref name=LNpde>{{Cite journal |last=Nirenberg |first=Louis |date=1959 |title=On elliptic partial differential equations |journal=Annali della Scuola Normale Superiore di Pisa |volume=3 |issue=13 |pages=115–162 |language=en-us}}</ref> Nonetheless, a complete proof of the inequality went missing in the literature for a long time. Indeed, to some extent, both original works of Gagliardo and Nirenberg do not contain a full and rigorous argument proving the result. For example, Nirenberg firstly included the inequality in a collection of lectures given in [[Pisa]] from September 1 to September 10, 1958. The transcription of the lectures was later published in 1959, and the author explicitly states only the main steps of the proof.<ref name=LNpde /> On the other hand, the proof of Gagliardo did not yield the result in full generality, i.e. for all possible values of the parameters appearing in the statement.<ref name="GNproof"/> Detailed proof in the whole [[Euclidean space]] were published in 2017<ref>{{cite book |last1=Leoni |first1=Giovanni |title=A first course in Sobolev spaces |date=2017 |publisher=American Mathematical Society |location=Providence, Rhode Island |isbn=978-1-4704-7702-8 |edition=Second}}</ref> and in 2021.<ref name="GNproof" />

From its original formulation, several mathematicians worked on proving and generalizing Gagliardo-Nirenberg type inequalities. The Italian mathematician [[Carlo Miranda]] developed a first generalization in 1963,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Miranda |first=Carlo |date=1963 |title=Su alcune disuguaglianze integrali |journal=Atti dell'Accademia Nazionale dei Lincei. Classe di Scienze Fisiche, Matematiche e Naturali |language=it |volume=8 |issue=7 |pages=1–14}}</ref> which was addressed and refined by Nirenberg later in 1966.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Nirenberg |first=Louis |date=1966 |title=On an extended interpolation inequality |journal=Annali della Scuola Normale Superiore di Pisa |volume=3 |issue=20 |pages=733–737}}</ref> The investigation of Gagliardo-Nirenberg type inequalities continued in the following decades. For instance, a careful study on negative exponents has been carried out extending the work of Nirenberg in 2018,<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Soudský |first1=Filip |last2=Molchanova |first2=Anastasia |last3=Roskovec |first3=Tomáš |date=2018 |title=Interpolation between Hölder and Lebesgue spaces with applications |journal=Journal of Mathematical Analysis and Applications |language=en |volume=466 |issue=1 |pages=160–168 |doi=10.1016/j.jmaa.2018.05.067|arxiv=1801.06865 |s2cid=119577652 |doi-access=free }}</ref> while Brezis and Mironescu characterized in full generality the embeddings between Sobolev spaces extending the inequality to fractional orders.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4" />

== Statement of the inequality ==

For any [[Extended real number line|extended real]] (i.e. possibly infinite) positive quantity <math> 1 \leq p \leq +\infty </math> and any integer <math>k \geq 1</math>, let <math> L^p(\mathbb{R}^n) </math> denote the usual [[Lp space|<math> L^p </math> spaces]], while <math> W^{k,p}(\mathbb{R}^n) </math> denotes the [[Sobolev space]] consisting of all real-valued functions in <math> L^p(\mathbb{R}^n) </math> such that all their weak derivatives up to order <math> k </math> are also in <math> L^p(\mathbb{R}^n) </math>. Both families of spaces are intended to be endowed with their standard norms, namely:<ref>{{Cite book |last=Brezis |first=Haim |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-0-387-70914-7 |title=Functional Analysis, Sobolev Spaces and Partial Differential Equations |publisher=Springer |year=2011 |location=New York |pages= |language=en |chapter= |doi=10.1007/978-0-387-70914-7|isbn=978-0-387-70913-0 }}</ref><math display="block">
\| u \|_{L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)} := 
\begin{cases}
\left( \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} |u|^p \right)^\frac{1}{p} & \quad \text{if } p < +\infty, \\
\underset{\mathbb{R}^n}{\operatorname{ess\,sup}} \,|u| & \quad \text{if } p = +\infty;
\end{cases} 
\qquad \qquad
\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb{R}^n)} := \begin{cases}
\left(\displaystyle\sum_{|\alpha| \leq k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)}^p\right)^\frac{1}{p} & \quad \text{if } p < +\infty, \\
 \ \ \ \displaystyle\sum_{|\alpha| \leq k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)} & \quad \text{if } p = +\infty;
\end{cases}

</math>
where <math> \operatorname{ess\,sup} </math> stands for [[Essential infimum and essential supremum|essential supremum]]. Above, for the sake of convenience, the same notation is used for scalar, vector and tensor-valued Lebesgue and Sobolev spaces.

The original version of the theorem, for functions defined on the whole Euclidean space <math>
\mathbb{R}^n

</math>, can be stated as follows.

{{Math theorem
| name = Theorem<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Nirenberg |first=Louis |date=1959 |title=On elliptic partial differential equations |journal=Annali della Scuola Normale Superiore di Pisa |volume=3 |issue=13 |pages=125 |language=en-us}}</ref>
| note = Gagliardo-Nirenberg
| math_statement = Let <math>1 \leq q \leq +\infty</math> be a positive extended real quantity. Let <math> j </math> and <math> m </math> be non-negative integers such that <math> j < m </math>. Furthermore, let <math> 1 \leq r \leq +\infty </math> be a positive extended real quantity, <math> p \geq 1 </math> be real and <math> \theta \in [0,1] </math> such that the relations
<math display=block>
\dfrac{1}{p} = \dfrac{j}{n} + \theta \left( \dfrac{1}{r} - \dfrac{m}{n} \right) + \dfrac{1-\theta}{q}, \qquad \dfrac jm \leq \theta \leq 1
</math>
hold. Then, 
<math display=block>
\|D^j u\|_{L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)} \leq C\|D^m u\|_{L^r(\mathbb{R}^n)}^\theta\|u\|_{L^q(\mathbb{R}^n)}^{1-\theta} </math>
for any <math> u \in L^q(\mathbb{R}^n) </math> such that <math> D^m u \in L^r(\mathbb{R}^n) </math>, with two exceptional cases:
# if <math> j = 0 </math> (with the understanding that <math> D^0 u = u </math>), <math> q = +\infty </math> and <math> rm < n </math>, then an additional assumption is needed: either <math> u </math> tends to 0 at infinity, or <math> u \in L^s(\mathbb{R}^n) </math> for some ''finite'' value of <math> s </math>;
# if <math> r > 1 </math> and <math> m - j - \frac{n}{r} </math> is a non-negative integer, then the additional assumption <math> \frac{j}{m}\leq\theta< 1 </math> (notice the strict inequality) is needed.
In any case, the constant <math> C > 0 </math> depends on the parameters <math> j,\,m,\,n,\,q,\,r,\,\theta </math>, but not on <math> u </math>.
}}Notice that the parameter <math>p</math> is determined uniquely by all the other ones and usually assumed to be finite.<ref name=":1" /> However, there are sharper formulations in which <math>p = +\infty</math> is considered (but other values may be excluded, for example <math>j = 0</math>).<ref name=":2" />

== Relevant corollaries of the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality ==
The Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality generalizes a collection of well-known results in the field of [[functional analysis]]. Indeed, given a suitable choice of the seven parameters appearing in the statement of the theorem, one obtains several useful and recurring inequalities in the theory of partial differential equations:

* The [[Sobolev embedding theorem]] establishes the existence of continuous embeddings between Sobolev spaces with different orders of differentiation and/or integrability. It can be obtained from the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality setting <math>\theta = 1</math> (so that the choice of <math>q</math> becomes irrelevant, and the same goes for the associated requirement <math>u \in L^q(\mathbb{R}^n)</math>) and the remaining parameters in such a way that <math display="block">\dfrac 1p - \dfrac jn = \dfrac 1r - \dfrac mn</math>and the other hypotheses are satisfied. The result reads then <math display="block">\|D^j u\|_{L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)} \leq C \|D^m u\|_{L^r(\mathbb{R}^n)}</math>for any <math>u</math> such that <math>D^m u \in L^r(\mathbb{R}^n)</math>. In particular, setting <math>j = 0</math> and <math>m = 1</math> yields that <math>p = r^*</math>, namely the [[Sobolev conjugate|Sobolev conjugate exponent]] of <math>r</math>, and we have the embedding <math display="block">W^{1,r}(\mathbb{R}^n) \hookrightarrow L^{r^*}(\mathbb{R}^n).</math>Notice that, in the embedding above, we also implicitly assume that <math>u \in L^r(\mathbb{R}^n)</math> and hence the first exceptional case does not apply.
* The [[Ladyzhenskaya's inequality|Ladyzhenskaya inequality]] is a special case of the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality. Considering the most common cases, namely <math>n = 2</math> and <math>n = 3</math>, we have the former corresponding to the parameter choice <math display="block">j = 0, \quad m = 1, \quad p = 4, \quad q = r = 2, \quad \theta = \frac 12,</math>yielding <math display="block">\|u\|_{L^4(\mathbb{R}^2)} \leq C\|u\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^2)}^\frac 12\|\nabla u\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^2)}^\frac 12</math>for any <math>u \in W^{1,2}(\mathbb{R}^2).</math> The constant <math>C</math> is universal and a possible (not sharp) value can be proven to be <math>\sqrt{2}</math>.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Galdi |first=Giovanni Paolo |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-0-387-09620-9 |title=An Introduction to the Mathematical Theory of the Navier-Stokes Equations. Steady-State Problems |series=Springer Monographs in Mathematics |publisher=Springer |year=2011 |edition=2nd |pages=55|doi=10.1007/978-0-387-09620-9 |isbn=978-0-387-09619-3 }}</ref><ref name="Br25">{{Cite book |last=Brasco |first=Lorenzo |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-031-87164-1 |title=Handbook of Calculus of Variations for Absolute Beginners|series=Unitext|publisher=Springer|year=2025|edition=1st|pages=602+xviii |doi=10.1007/978-3-031-87164-1|isbn=978-3-031-87164-1}}</ref> In three space dimensions, a slightly different choice of parameters is needed, namely<math display="block">j = 0, \quad m = 1, \quad p = 4, \quad q = r = 2, \quad \theta = \frac 34,</math>yielding<math display="block">\|u\|_{L^4(\mathbb{R}^3)} \leq C\|u\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)}^\frac 14\|\nabla u\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)}^\frac 34</math>for any <math>u \in W^{1,2}(\mathbb{R}^3)</math>. Here, it holds <math>C = \left( \frac{4\sqrt 3}{9}\right)^\frac 34</math>.<ref name=":0" />
* The Nash inequality, which was published by [[John Forbes Nash Jr.|John Nash]] in 1958, is yet another result generalized by the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality. Indeed, choosing<math display="block">j = 0, \quad m = 1, \quad n \geq 1,\quad p = 2, \quad q = 1, \quad r = 2, \quad \theta = \frac{n}{n+2},</math>one gets <math display="block">\|u\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)} \leq C \|u\|_{L^1(\mathbb{R}^n)}^{\frac{2}{n+2}}\|\nabla u\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)}^{\frac{n}{n+2}}</math>which is oftentimes recast as<math display="block">\|u\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)}^{1+\frac 2n} \leq C \|u\|_{L^1(\mathbb{R}^n)}^{\frac{2}{n}}\|\nabla u\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)}</math>or its squared version.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Nash |first=John |date=1958 |title=Continuity of solutions of parabolic and elliptic equations |journal=American Journal of Mathematics |volume=80 |issue=4 |pages=931–954|doi=10.2307/2372841 |jstor=2372841 |bibcode=1958AmJM...80..931N }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bouin |first1=Emeric |last2=Dolbeault |first2=Jean |last3=Schmeiser |first3=Christian |date=2020 |title=A variational proof of Nash's inequality |journal= Rendiconti Lincei, Matematica e Applicazioni|volume=31 |issue=1 |pages=211–223 |doi=10.4171/RLM/886|arxiv=1811.12770 |bibcode=2020RLSFN..31..211B |s2cid=119668382 |url=https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-01940110/file/BDS-2018-Nash.pdf }}</ref>

== Proof of the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality ==
A complete and detailed proof of the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality has been missing in literature for a long time since its first statements. Indeed, both original works of Gagliardo and Nirenberg lacked some details, or even presented only the main steps of the proof.<ref name=GNproof>{{Cite journal |last1=Fiorenza |first1=Alberto |last2=Formica |first2=Maria Rosaria |last3=Roskovec |first3=Tomáš |last4=Soudský |first4=Filip |date=2021 |title=Detailed Proof of Classical Gagliardo–Nirenberg Interpolation Inequality with Historical Remarks |url=https://www.ems-ph.org/doi/10.4171/ZAA/1681 |journal=Zeitschrift für Analysis und ihre Anwendungen |language=en |volume=40 |issue=2 |pages=217–236 |doi=10.4171/ZAA/1681 |arxiv=1812.04281 |s2cid=119708752 |issn=0232-2064}}</ref>

The most delicate point concerns the limiting case <math display="inline">\theta = \frac{j}{m}</math>. In order to avoid the two exceptional cases, we further assume that <math>r</math> is finite and that <math>u \in W^{m,r}(\mathbb{R}^n)</math>, so in particular <math>u \in L^r(\mathbb{R}^n)</math>. The core of the proof is based on two [[Mathematical induction|proofs by induction]].

{{Collapse top|title=Sketch of the proof of the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality<ref name=GNproof />}}
Throughout the proof, given <math> j </math> and <math> m </math>, we shall assume that <math display=inline> \theta = \frac jm</math>. A double induction argument is applied to the couple of integers <math> (j,m) </math>, representing the orders of differentiation. The other parameters are constructed in such a way that they comply with the hypotheses of the theorem. As base case, we assume that the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality holds for <math> j = 1 </math> and <math> m = 2 </math> (hence <math display=inline> \theta = \frac 12 </math>). Here, in order for the inequality to hold, the remaining parameters should satisfy <math display=block>
\dfrac 2p = \dfrac 1r + \dfrac 1q, \qquad n \geq 1. 
</math>
The first induction step goes as follows. Assume the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality holds for some <math> m = m^\star \in \mathbb{N} </math> strictly greater than <math> 1 </math> and <math> j = 1</math> (hence <math display=inline> \theta = \frac{1}{m^\star} </math>). We are going to prove that it also holds for <math> m = m^\star + 1 </math> and <math> j = 1 </math> (with <math display=inline> \theta = \frac{1}{m^\star+1} </math>). To this end, the remaining parameters <math> n,\,p,\,q,\,r </math> necessarily satisfy <math display=block>
\dfrac 1p = \dfrac{\frac{1}{m^\star+1}}{r} + \dfrac{\frac{m^\star}{m^\star+1}}{q}, \qquad n \geq 1.
</math>
Fix them as such. Then, let <math> s > 0 </math> be such that <math display=block>
\dfrac 2p = \dfrac 1s + \dfrac 1q.
</math>
From the base case, we can infer that <math display = block>
\|\nabla u\|_{L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)} \leq C\|D^2 u\|^{\frac 12}_{L^s(\mathbb{R}^n)}\|u\|_{L^q(\mathbb{R}^n)}^{\frac 12}.
</math>
Now, from the two relations between the parameters, through some algebraic manipulations we arrive at <math display=block>
\dfrac 1s = \dfrac{\frac{1}{m^\star}}{r} + \dfrac{\frac{m^\star-1}{m^\star}}{p}, \qquad n \geq 1, </math>
therefore the inequality with <math> m = m^\star </math> applied to <math> \nabla u </math> implies <math display = block>
\|D^2 u\|_{L^s(\mathbb{R}^n)} \leq C\|D^{m^\star+1} u\|^{\frac{1}{m^\star}}_{L^r(\mathbb{R}^n)}\|\nabla u\|_{L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)}^{\frac{m^\star-1}{m^\star}}.
</math>
The two inequalities imply the sought Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality, namely <math display=block>
\|\nabla u\|_{L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)} \leq C\|D^{m^\star+1} u\|^{\frac{1}{m^\star+1}}_{L^r(\mathbb{R}^n)}\|u\|_{L^q(\mathbb{R}^n)}^{\frac{m^\star}{m^\star+1}},
</math>
The second induction step is similar, but allows <math> j </math> to change. Assume the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality holds for some pair <math> (j^\star, m^\star) \in \mathbb{N}^2 </math> with <math> j^\star < m^\star </math> (hence <math display=inline> \theta = \frac{j^\star}{m^\star} </math>). It is enough to prove that it also holds for <math> m = m^\star + 1 </math> and <math> j = j^\star+1 </math> (with <math display=inline> \theta = \frac{j^\star+1}{m^\star+1} </math>). Again, fix the parameters <math> n,\,p,\,q,\,r </math> in such a way that <math display=block>
\dfrac 1p = \dfrac{\frac{j^\star+1}{m^\star+1}}{r} + \dfrac{\frac{m^\star-j^\star}{m^\star+1}}{q}, \qquad n \geq 1,
</math>
and let <math> t </math> be such that <math display=block>
\dfrac 1p = \dfrac{\frac{j^\star}{m^\star}}{r} + \dfrac{\frac{m^\star-j^\star}{m^\star}}{t}.
</math>
The inequality with <math> j = j^\star </math> and <math> m = m^\star </math> applied to <math> \nabla u </math> entails <math display = block>
\|D^{j^\star+1} u\|_{L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)} \leq C\|D^{m^\star+1} u\|^{\frac{j^\star}{m^\star}}_{L^r(\mathbb{R}^n)}\|\nabla u\|_{L^t(\mathbb{R}^n)}^{\frac{m^\star-j^\star}{m^\star}}.
</math>
Since, by the first induction step, we can assume the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality holds with <math> m = j^\star + 1 </math> and <math> j = 1 </math>, we get <math display = block>
\|\nabla u\|_{L^t(\mathbb{R}^n)} \leq C\|D^{j^\star+1} u\|^{\frac{1}{j^\star+1}}_{L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)}\|u\|_{L^q(\mathbb{R}^n)}^{\frac{j^\star}{j^\star+1}}.
</math>
The proof is completed by combining the two inequalities. In order to prove the base case, several technical lemmas are necessary, while the remaining values of <math> \theta </math> can be recovered by interpolation and a proof can be found, for instance, in the original work of Nirenberg.<ref name=LNpde />
{{Collapse bottom|}}

== The Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality in bounded domains ==
In many problems coming from the theory of partial differential equations, one has to deal with functions whose domain is not the whole Euclidean space <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math>, but rather some given bounded, [[Open set|open]] and [[Connected space|connected]] set <math>\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n.</math> In the following, we also assume that <math>\Omega</math> has finite [[Lebesgue measure]] and satisfies the [[cone condition]] (among those are the widely used [[Lipschitz domain]]s). Both Gagliardo and Nirenberg found out that their theorem could be extended to this case adding a penalization term to the right hand side. Precisely,

{{Math theorem
| name = Theorem<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Nirenberg |first=Louis |date=1959 |title=On elliptic partial differential equations |journal=Annali della Scuola Normale Superiore di Pisa |volume=3 |issue=13 |pages=126 |language=en-us}}</ref>
| note = Gagliardo-Nirenberg in bounded domains
| math_statement = Let <math> \Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n </math> be a measurable, bounded, open and connected domain satisfying the cone condition. Let <math>1 \leq q \leq +\infty</math> be a positive extended real quantity. Let <math> j </math> and <math> m </math> be non-negative integers such that <math> j < m </math>. Furthermore, let <math> 1 \leq r \leq +\infty </math> be a positive extended real quantity, <math> p \geq 1 </math> be real and <math> \theta \in [0,1] </math> such that the relations
<math display=block>
\dfrac{1}{p} = \dfrac{j}{n} + \theta \left( \dfrac{1}{r} - \dfrac{m}{n} \right) + \dfrac{1-\theta}{q}, \qquad \dfrac jm \leq \theta \leq 1
</math>
hold. Then, 
<math display=block>
\|D^j u\|_{L^p(\Omega)} \leq C\|D^m u\|_{L^r(\Omega)}^\theta\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}^{1-\theta} + C\|u\|_{L^\sigma(\Omega)} </math> 
where <math> u \in L^q(\Omega) </math> such that <math> D^m u \in L^r(\Omega) </math> and <math> \sigma </math> is arbitrary, with one exceptional case:
# if <math> r > 1 </math> and <math> m - j - \frac{n}{r} </math> is a non-negative integer, then the additional assumption <math> \frac{j}{m}\leq \theta <1 </math> (notice the strict inequality) is needed.
In any case, the constant <math> C > 0 </math> depends on the parameters <math> j,\,m,\,n,\,q,\,r,\,\theta </math>, on the domain <math> \Omega </math>, but not on <math> u </math>.
}}

The necessity of a different formulation with respect to the case <math>\Omega = \mathbb{R}^n</math> is rather straightforward to prove. Indeed, since <math>\Omega</math> has finite Lebesgue measure, any affine function belongs to <math>L^p(\Omega)</math> for every <math>p</math> (including <math>p = +\infty</math>). Of course, it holds much more: affine functions belong to <math>C^\infty(\Omega)</math> and all their derivatives of order greater than or equal to two are identically equal to zero in <math>\Omega</math>. It can be easily seen that the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality for the case <math>\Omega = \mathbb{R}^n</math> fails to be true for any non constant affine function, since a contradiction is immediately achieved when <math>j = 1</math> and <math>m \geq 2</math> , and therefore cannot hold in general for integrable functions defined on bounded domains.

That being said, under slightly stronger assumptions, it is possible to recast the theorem in such a way that the penalization term is "absorbed" in the first term at right hand side. Indeed, if <math>u \in L^q(\Omega) \cap W^{m,r}(\Omega)</math>, then one can choose <math>\sigma = \min(r,q)</math> and get <math display="block">\begin{align}
\|D^j u\|_{L^p(\Omega)} & \leq C\|D^m u\|_{L^r(\Omega)}^\theta\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}^{1-\theta}+C\|u\|_{L^{\min(r,q)}(\Omega)}^\theta\|u\|_{L^{\min(r,q)}(\Omega)}^{1-\theta} \\
& \leq C\|u\|_{W^{m,r}(\Omega)}^\theta\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}^{1-\theta}.
\end{align}</math>This formulation has the advantage of recovering the structure of the theorem in the full Euclidean space, with the only caution that the Sobolev [[seminorm]] is replaced by the full <math>W^{m,r}</math>-norm. For this reason, the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality in bounded domains is commonly stated in this way.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Brezis |first=Haim |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-0-387-70914-7 |title=Functional Analysis, Sobolev Spaces and Partial Differential Equations |publisher=Springer |year=2011 |location=New York |pages=233 |language=en |chapter= |doi=10.1007/978-0-387-70914-7|isbn=978-0-387-70913-0 }}</ref>

Finally, observe that the first exceptional case appearing in the statement of the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality for the whole space is no longer relevant in bounded domains, since for [[finite measure]] sets we have that <math>L^\infty(\Omega) \hookrightarrow L^\rho(\Omega)</math> for any finite <math>\rho \geq 1.</math>

== Generalization to non-integer orders ==

The problem of interpolating different Sobolev spaces has been solved in full generality by [[Haïm Brezis]] and [[Petru Mironescu]] in two works dated 2018 and 2019.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last1=Brezis |first1=Haïm |last2=Mironescu |first2=Petru |date=2018 |title=Gagliardo–Nirenberg inequalities and non-inequalities: The full story |url=https://ems.press/journals/aihpc/articles/4077138 |journal=Annales de l'Institut Henri Poincaré C |language=en |volume=35 |issue=5 |pages=1355–1376 |doi=10.1016/j.anihpc.2017.11.007 |bibcode=2018AIHPC..35.1355B |s2cid=58891735 |issn=0294-1449|doi-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last1=Brezis |first1=Haïm |last2=Mironescu |first2=Petru |date=2019-10-15 |title=Where Sobolev interacts with Gagliardo–Nirenberg |journal=Journal of Functional Analysis |language=en |volume=277 |issue=8 |pages=2839–2864 |doi=10.1016/j.jfa.2019.02.019 |s2cid=128179938 |issn=0022-1236|doi-access=free }}</ref> Furthermore, their results do not depend on the dimension <math>n</math> and allow real values of <math>j</math> and <math>m</math>, rather than integer. Here, <math>\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n</math> is either the full space, a half-space or a bounded and Lipschitz domain. If <math>s \in (0,1)</math> and <math>p \geq 1</math> is an extended real quantity, the space <math>W^{s,p}(\Omega)</math> is defined by<math display="block">W^{s,p}(\Omega):= \begin{cases}
\left\{ u \in L^p(\Omega): \dfrac{|u(x)-u(y)|}{|x-y|^{s+\frac np}} \in L^p(\Omega \times \Omega) \right\} & \quad \text{if } p < +\infty,\\
\left\{ u \in L^\infty(\Omega): \dfrac{|u(x)-u(y)|}{|x-y|^{s}} \in L^\infty(\Omega \times \Omega) \right\} & \quad \text{if } p = +\infty;\\
\end{cases}</math>and endowed with the norm<math display="block">\|u\|_{W^{s,p}(\Omega)} := \begin{cases}
\left(\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p + \displaystyle\int_\Omega \int_\Omega \dfrac{|u(x)-u(y)|^p}{|x-y|^{n+sp}}\right)^\frac{1}{p} & \quad \text{if } p<+\infty,\\
\|u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)} + \left\| \dfrac{u(x)-u(y)}{(x-y)^{s}}\right\|_{L^\infty(\Omega \times \Omega)} &  \quad \text{if } p=+\infty.
\end{cases}</math>If <math>s \geq 1</math>, then we set <math display="block">W^{s,p}(\Omega) := \{ u \in W^{\lfloor s \rfloor,p}(\Omega) : D^{\lfloor s \rfloor}u \in W^{\{s\},p}(\Omega)\}, \qquad \|u\|_{W^{s,p}(\Omega)} := \begin{cases}
\left(\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p + \|D^{\lfloor s \rfloor}u\|_{W^{\{s\},p}(\Omega)}^p\right)^\frac{1}{p} & \quad \text{if } p<+\infty,\\
\|u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)} + \|D^{\lfloor s \rfloor}u\|_{W^{\{s\},\infty}(\Omega)} &  \quad \text{if } p=+\infty;
\end{cases}</math>where <math>\lfloor s \rfloor</math> and <math>\{s\}</math> denote the [[Floor and ceiling functions|integer part]] and the [[fractional part]] of <math>s</math>, respectively, i.e. <math>s = \lfloor s \rfloor + \{s\}</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Di Nezza |first1=Eleonora |last2=Palatucci |first2=Giampiero |last3=Valdinoci |first3=Enrico |date=2012 |title=Hitchhikerʼs guide to the fractional Sobolev spaces |journal=Bulletin des Sciences Mathématiques |language=en |volume=136 |issue=5 |pages=524 |doi=10.1016/j.bulsci.2011.12.004 |arxiv=1104.4345 |s2cid=55443959 |issn=0007-4497|doi-access=free }}</ref> In this definition, there is the understanding that <math>W^{0,p}(\Omega) = L^p(\Omega)</math>, so that the usual Sobolev spaces are recovered whenever <math>s</math> is a positive integer. These spaces are often referred to as fractional Sobolev spaces. A generalization of the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality to these spaces reads
{{Math theorem
| name = Theorem<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Brezis |first1=Haïm |last2=Mironescu |first2=Petru |date=2018 |title=Gagliardo–Nirenberg inequalities and non-inequalities: The full story |url=https://ems.press/journals/aihpc/articles/4077138 |journal=Annales de l'Institut Henri Poincaré C |language=en |volume=35 |issue=5 |page=1356|doi=10.1016/j.anihpc.2017.11.007 |bibcode=2018AIHPC..35.1355B |s2cid=58891735 |issn=0294-1449|doi-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref>
| note = Brezis-Mironescu
| math_statement = Let <math> \Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n</math> be either the whole space, a half-space or a bounded Lipschitz domain. Let <math>1 \leq p,\, p_1,\, p_2 \leq +\infty</math> be three positive extended real quantities and let <math> s,\,s_1,\,s_2</math> be non-negative real numbers. Furthermore, let <math> \theta \in (0,1) </math> and assume that
<math display=block>
s_1 \leq s_2, \qquad s = \theta s_1 + (1-\theta)s_2, \qquad \dfrac{1}{p} = \dfrac{\theta}{p_1} + \dfrac{1-\theta}{p_2}
</math>
hold. Then, 
<math display=block>
\|u\|_{W^{s,p}(\Omega)} \leq C\|u\|_{W^{s_1,p_1}(\Omega)}^\theta\|u\|_{W^{s_2,p_2}(\Omega)}^{1-\theta} </math>
for any <math> u \in W^{s_1,p_1}(\Omega) \cap W^{s_2,p_2}(\Omega)</math> if and only if
<math display=block> \text{at least one of} \quad \begin{cases}
s_2 \in \mathbb{N} \text{ and } s_2 \geq 1, \\
p_2 = 1, \\
0 < s_2-s_1 \leq 1 - \displaystyle \dfrac{1}{p_1}
\end{cases} \quad \text{is false.} </math>
The constant <math> C > 0 </math> depends on the parameters <math> p,\,p_1,\,p_2,\,s,\,s_1,\,s_2,\,\theta </math>, on the domain <math> \Omega </math>, but not on <math> u </math>.
}}For example, the parameter choice <math display="block">p = \dfrac 83, \quad p_1 = 2, \quad p_2 = 4, \quad s = \dfrac{7}{12},\quad s_1 = \dfrac 12, \quad s_2 = \dfrac 23, \quad \theta = \dfrac 12</math>gives the estimate <math display="block">\|u\|_{W^{\frac{7}{12}, \frac 83}(\Omega)} \leq C\|u\|_{W^{\frac{1}{2}, 2}(\Omega)}^\frac{1}{2}\|u\|_{W^{\frac{2}{3}, 4}(\Omega)}^{\frac{1}{2}}.</math>The validity of the estimate is granted, for instance, from the fact that <math>p_2 \neq 1</math>.
